prompts.question: Compare the speed of the mass at point A to that at point B. Support your answer using appropriate mathematical relationships.
markerNotes: Measure the heights of A and B from the same reference level, the bottom of the circle.
Write the total mechanical energy at each point, set them equal, and solve for the speed at A.
A comparison needs a relationship such as vA = √3 vB, not just faster or slower.
commonStudentErrors: Says the speed is the same at A and B because the string length is the same.
Measures the heights of A and B from different reference levels.
States that A is faster, without any mathematical comparison.
prompts.markingCriteria:

sampleAnswers.answer:
The speed of the ball at point A will be greater than v from part (a).
Total mechanical energy = Ek + GPE
At point B:
Total mechanical energy = ½ × m × gr + mg(2r) = total mechanical energy at A
At A the gravitational potential energy = mgr and thus ½ × m × gr + 2mgr = mgr + EkA
Simplifying gives EkA = 1.5mgr = ½ mvA²
And finally vA = √(3gr) = √3 vB
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: energy is conserved between A and B, the heights are set from the bottom of the circle, and the speeds are compared as vA = √3 vB. A middle answer compares the speeds through energy but gives no mathematical relationship.

sampleAnswers.answer: Point A is lower than point B, so the speed at A is greater. As the mass falls from B to A, gravitational potential energy converts to kinetic energy, and total mechanical energy is conserved.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by comparing the speeds at A and B through conservation of energy. It gives no mathematical relationship between the speeds, and writing the energy at each point and solving for vA = √3 vB would lift it to the 3-mark row.

prompts.question: What minimum speed is required for the rider to land on the second ramp?
markerNotes: Resolve the launch velocity into horizontal and vertical components before writing any equation.
The same time t applies to both directions, so eliminate t to find u.
Both ramps are 2 m high, so the vertical displacement from launch to landing is zero.
commonStudentErrors: Uses the full launch speed in both directions without resolving the 20° launch angle.
Writes only the horizontal equation and so cannot eliminate the time.
Uses the wrong sign for gravity in the vertical equation, which gives a negative speed.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Calculates the minimum speed required for the rider to land on the second ramp
3 marks: Provides substantial working to calculate the minimum speed
2 marks: Makes progress towards determining the minimum speed
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
To calculate u:
In the horizontal direction, sx = uxt with ux = ucos(θ), so t = sx/ucos(θ)
In the vertical direction, 0 = uyt + ½ayt² with uy = usin(θ), so u = −ayt/2sin(θ)
Substituting into the equation for u gives, u² = −aysx/2cos(θ)sin(θ) or u = √(−aysx/2cos(θ)sin(θ))
For ay = −9.8, sx = 16 and θ = 20
u = 15.6 m s⁻¹
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: the horizontal and vertical equations are combined to eliminate time, and the values substituted to give 15.6 m s⁻¹. A middle answer stops before the vertical motion is used.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Horizontally, sx = u cos 20° × t, so t = 16/(u cos 20°).
Vertically, the rider lands at the same height as the launch, so the vertical displacement is zero.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by making progress: the horizontal equation and the zero vertical displacement are set up. The vertical equation is not solved and the speed is not found, and using both equations to eliminate t would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The rider must cover 16 m horizontally.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information, the horizontal distance. Writing the horizontal equation with the launch velocity resolved would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse the subsequent motion of BOTH ma and mb after the explosion. Include reference to relevant conservation laws and formulae in your answer.
markerNotes: Use conservation of momentum to find both velocities immediately after the explosion before discussing their motion.
Compare ma's speed, 2v, with the escape speed √(2GM/r) to decide whether ma escapes, and say why it does not return.
Describe mb's motion from zero velocity at Y as it accelerates towards Earth, and apply conservation of energy.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the pieces' motion without applying conservation of momentum or a formula.
Says ma will fall back to Earth because it is in orbit.
Says mb continues in its original orbit at the original speed.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Comprehensively analyses the motion of both pieces with reference to relevant conservation laws and formulae
6-7 marks: Analyses features of the motion of both pieces with reference to relevant conservation laws and formulae
4-5 marks: Describes a feature of the motion of each piece OR describes features of the motion of one piece; Applies a conservation law and a relevant formula
2-3 marks: Describes a feature of the motion of a piece; Identifies a relevant conservation law and/or refers to a relevant equation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
By the law of conservation of momentum, the momentum changes of ma and mb resulting from the force produced by the explosion must be equal but opposite.
Since they are of equal mass, the velocity change of both pieces, must be the same, but in opposite directions. Since the velocity of ma increases by v in the direction in which it was travelling, the velocity of mb, is also v, but in the opposite direction to which it was travelling.
Hence, relative to the Earth, the velocity of mb must become zero at that instant.
The orbital velocity of the satellite prior to the explosion is given by vorbital = √(GM/r)
Hence the instantaneous velocity of ma as a result of the explosion is double the orbital velocity before the explosion because 2v = 2√(GM/r) > the escape velocity vesc = √(2GM/r) the velocity of ma after the explosion is greater than the escape velocity.
After the explosion, the pieces ma will continue travel away from Earth at a decreasing velocity, however because its initial velocity exceeds the escape velocity from the explosion point, it will never stop or return to Earth. Its total energy (kinetic + potential) remains constant and will always be positive.
Consequently, mb will begin to accelerate, from an initial velocity of zero, towards the centre of Earth. Its acceleration is initially less than 9.8 m s⁻² because it is not at Earth’s surface.
As the force due to gravity on mb increases, its acceleration increases and so its velocity towards the centre of Earth increases at an increasing rate until it reaches Earth’s atmosphere.
Consistent with the law of conservation of energy, until mb reaches Earth’s atmosphere, the sum of its kinetic and potential energy must remain constant and equal to its initial potential energy at the instant after the explosion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 8-mark row: conservation of momentum gives mb's velocity, and the orbital and escape speeds show that ma escapes while mb falls back, with the energy and formulae applied. The middle answer applies these to each piece but does not analyse mb's fall in terms of energy.

sampleAnswers.answer:
By conservation of momentum, the total momentum of the satellite is unchanged by the explosion. The changes in momentum of ma and mb are therefore equal and opposite. Since the two pieces have equal mass, the velocity change of ma, which is v, must be matched by a change of −v for mb, so mb is left with zero velocity relative to Earth.
The orbital speed before the explosion is v = √(GM/r). The speed of ma after the explosion is 2v, which is more than the speed needed for a circular orbit at that distance, so gravity cannot keep ma in its orbit and it moves further away from Earth.
Because mb starts from rest, gravity pulls it straight towards Earth. It speeds up as it falls, and its acceleration grows as it moves closer to Earth’s centre.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-5 mark row by describing a feature of the motion of each piece and applying conservation of momentum with the orbital speed formula, v = √(GM/r). It does not analyse whether ma escapes: comparing 2v with the escape speed, √(2GM/r) = √2 v, would settle it. It also does not apply conservation of energy to the fall of mb. Adding both would lift it to the 6-7 row.

The photon model of light explains the trend by stating that light consists of discrete packets of energy called photons. The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency (E = hf). When photons strike the metal, they transfer energy to electrons. If the photon energy exceeds the work function of the metal, the threshold frequency is exceeded and electrons are ejected with kinetic energy proportional to the excess energy (KE = hf – ϕ).

sampleAnswers.answer:
The two postulates of special relativity are: the speed of light in a vacuum is an absolute constant, and all inertial frames of reference are equivalent.
The consequences of these postulates are time dilation, length contraction and relativistic momentum dilation. Time dilation means that the measured time between events increases as the speed of an observer increases. Length contraction means that the length of an object decreases as the speed of an observer increases, and relativistic momentum dilation means that objects (with mass) cannot travel at c as it takes increasing amounts of energy to accelerate objects as they approach the speed of light.
Length contraction and time dilation can both be seen in observations of muons at Earth’s surface. The short half-life of muons suggests that there should be very few of them that arrive at Earth’s surface from their point of origin high in Earth’s atmosphere, but the muon flux is greater than suggested by half-life and distance travelled alone. However, when the distance travelled is considered from the muon’s frame of reference, it is length-contracted according to l = l₀√(1 − v²/c²), giving an effective shorter distance for them to travel. From the perspective of an observer on Earth’s surface, the time taken for them to decay is dilated, giving an effective greater amount of time for them to travel before decaying.
The effects of relativistic momentum can be seen in particle accelerators in terms of the increasing amounts of energy to required to accelerate the particles as they approach the speed of light – it is though the objects are much more massive than they are.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 8-mark row: the postulates are used to analyse time dilation, length contraction and relativistic momentum for different observers, with muon and particle evidence. The middle answer analyses time and length with one piece of evidence but does not analyse motion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Special relativity rests on two postulates: the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, and the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. One consequence is time dilation. A moving clock runs slow when observed from a frame in which it moves, so the time between events is longer for that observer. Another is length contraction, in which a moving object is shorter along its direction of motion. Muons created high in the atmosphere reach the ground in greater numbers than their short half-life predicts, which is evidence for time dilation as seen from Earth.

sampleAnswers.answer: Special relativity says the speed of light is the same for all observers, and that moving clocks run slow. Experiments with fast particles have confirmed time dilation.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Experiments and theoretical ideas have both been critical in the development of the Standard Model of matter.
Particle accelerators have been used to verify key ideas about fundamental particles and the structure of matter. Particle accelerators allow for small wavelength ‘matter probes’ at high energies, giving high resolution for probing the structure of matter.
Examples of particle accelerator use in the development of the Standard Model include:
• Verification of the electroweak theory, which says that the electromagnetic and weak nuclear forces are a result of the same interaction.
• The discovery of a Higgs Boson, many decades after it was first proposed as necessary in explaining the mass of particles.
• Verification of the existence of quarks by showing the protons and neutrons have internal structure.
Earlier experiments used simpler equipment such as the cloud chamber which was used to discover antimatter following its earlier theoretical prediction.
Many experiments have verified earlier theoretical ideas, and these confirmations have then in turn allowed the proposal of further ideas, which have in turn later been verified by experiments.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: the answer analyses how accelerator tests of electroweak theory, the Higgs boson and quark structure fed into the Standard Model. The middle answer describes the accelerator results and links them to the model without showing how theory and experiment shaped each other.

sampleAnswers.answer: Particle accelerators collide particles at high energies, and the collisions convert energy into mass. The results have revealed quarks, leptons and force-carrying bosons. In the late 1960s, electrons fired at protons showed that protons have internal structure. The Higgs boson, which is linked to the mass of particles, was found at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider in 2012. These discoveries fit the Standard Model, which groups all known fundamental particles into quarks, leptons and bosons.
